h2: A year of work, then a week in Florida.
Want to know more about RoboBoat?
p: An international student competition in Florida. Teams build small autonomous boats and let them solve a course on the water, with no one steering.
RoboBoat is run by RoboNation in the USA. Student teams from all over the world design, build and test their own autonomous surface vessel, and then bring it to Florida.
The tasks are based on work boats do at sea, like watching a coastline or keeping a port safe. The boats are judged on how they move, how they are built and what they carry on board.
RoboBoat 2026 was the 19th competition. It was held from 19 to 24 February at Nathan Benderson Park in Sarasota, Florida.
Teams work on their boats for most of the year before the competition week.
Teams read the rules and then design, build and test their own small autonomous boat during the year.
In Florida the boat has to run a set course on its own. The team is not allowed to steer it.
Every team hands in a technical report and a video, and presents the boat to the judges.
Points come from the course, the design and the documents. The team with the most points wins.

RoboBoat is one of the biggest competitions for autonomous boats in the world. Teams we meet at Njord sail here too, for example Navier USN from Norway and AGH Solar Boat from Poland. The skills are the same ones we build with Argus: find the way, see what is around the boat, and dock on your own.

/competitions/njord-challange.title: Marinor NTNU
h2: What is out on the course.
Want to know more about Njord?
p: A student competition for autonomous boats, held every August in Trondheim. Teams from several countries bring boats they have built and let them sail on their own.
Njord: The Autonomous Ship Challenge is run by Njord NTNU, a student organisation started in Trondheim in 2019. Every August student teams come to Nyhavna in Trondheim.

Each team builds and runs its own autonomous boat. During the week the boats solve tasks on the water with no one steering. In 2025 eleven teams from eight countries took part, and Navier USN from Norway won.
The boats sail a course in the harbour and get one task at a time. The team is not allowed to steer.
The boat has to steer through a marked course on the water and show that it can control its own movement.
The boat has to read the sea markers and find its own way through the course, without help from the team.
Another vessel crosses the path. The boat has to see it in time and go around it safely.
The last task is to find the right spot at the dock and park the boat there on its own.
The course has the same kind of marks a boat meets at sea, and the boat has to read them.
Floating markers that show where the course goes and where the boat must not sail.
Sea marks that tell you which side is safe to pass, just like in real shipping.
Printed markers the boat reads with its camera to find the right dock or gate.
A small vessel from the organisers that moves across the course in the collision task.
The jury also gives points for the report, the presentation and the inspection.
Most points come from what the boat actually does on the water during the week.
The team writes about the design and the choices behind the boat.
Every team presents their work for the jury and the other teams.
The boat is checked against the rules for size, safety and power before it may sail.
Teams show the data and the interface they use to follow the boat.
There are also prizes for team spirit, sportsmanship and best presentation.
Marinor NTNU is on the team list for the Njord Challenge 2026. We built Argus for these four tasks: find the way, see what is around it, avoid other boats and dock.

/about.title: Marinor NTNU
h2: What we have done so far.
From the workshop and the harbour.
p: Marinor NTNU is a student organisation at NTNU in Trondheim. We build autonomous boats and enter them in student competitions.
We build our boats in the workshop and test them in the harbour in Trondheim.
Marinor NTNU is a technical student organisation at NTNU. We build autonomous boats that find their way on the water without anyone steering.
Our members study robotics, automation, marine technology and other subjects. We work with the Department of Engineering Cybernetics.
Marinor was founded in 2025 and has more than 35 members.
We started in 2025. Here is what we have done and what we plan next.
Four students start Marinor NTNU in Trondheim. The first members build the hulls for Argus in the workshop.
We sail Argus in Njord: The Autonomous Ship Challenge in Trondheim, against university teams from several countries.
In 2027 we want to win the Njord Challenge. After that we want to enter RoboBoat in Florida.
In 2028 we plan to start building a much bigger boat. The long-term goal is a boat that can sail the Norwegian coast on its own with a crew on board.
In the long run we want to scale up our competition boat. The goal is a boat that sails the whole Norwegian coast on its own, with people on board.
Members make the hulls, electronics and software themselves and test them in the harbour.
We work with the Department of Engineering Cybernetics and with companies that support us.
Members get to know other students, researchers and companies that work with autonomous boats.
We need students in software, electronics, mechanics, design and more. You do not need any boat experience.

/projects/argus.title: Marinor NTNU
p: Our first autonomous boat. A catamaran built by students in Trondheim and tested in the harbour.
Argus is our first autonomous surface vessel. It finds its way on the water with no one at the wheel.
The hulls, electronics, sensors, control system and software all have to work together on one boat. Our members made every part of it.
The sensors and hardware Argus uses to see, find its position and steer.
Argus is a catamaran. The two hulls give a wide and stable platform for the sensors and electronics.
With four propellers Argus can turn a full 360 degrees while it keeps moving forward.
A GNSS-aided inertial navigation system. It combines multi-frequency GNSS receivers with gyroscopes and accelerometers, and gives Argus its position, heading, speed, roll and pitch.
Two lenses measure the distance to things in front of the boat. The images are also used to recognise what the objects are.
Measures the distance to docks, buoys, boats and other obstacles around the boat.
Controls the motors. It calculates the PWM signal that sets the speed of each propeller.
Sends all data from the boat to land, so we can follow its internal state while it sails.
The computer, power and wiring are kept dry inside one sealed case.
From what the sensors see to the signal that turns the propellers, in the order it happens on board.
The depth camera measures distance and recognises objects like buoys and boats. The LiDAR measures the distance to everything around the boat.

GNSS receivers give the position and heading. Gyroscopes and accelerometers fill in between the satellite fixes and keep the estimate going if the signal drops out. Correction data over 5G makes the position more accurate.
What the sensors find goes into a map of the water around the boat. Obstacles, and the water close to them, cost more to sail through.
Keeps track of what Argus is doing right now, for example following the course, going around another boat or docking, and switches when something changes.
The path planning algorithm finds the cheapest route across the cost map, and plans again when the map changes.
The flight controller turns the plan into PWM signals for the four motors.
All data from Argus is sent to land over 5G, so we can follow its internal state and get important information while it sails.

Long days of sanding, filling and painting to make the hulls smooth and watertight.
The first float test in the harbour. Does it float? It does.
Hulls, frame and electronics are joined together on the dock for the first time.
Argus goes into the water with all sensors on board – ready for testing.
